original_question: Can motivic integration, or a suitable stringy invariant, be used to prove a Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich type formula in the wild setting?
target_in_paper: Problem 11.2 in Section 11 (“Relation to other theories on wild ramification”): “Can we show a Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich type formula by using motivic integration and/or a version of stringy invariant?”
correct_elements: Your draft captures the exact mathematical nucleus of the paper’s target problem: a Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich-type formula in the context of wild ramification, with motivic integration and stringy invariants as the proposed tools. It also correctly keeps the question open-ended rather than adding hypotheses or narrowing to a special class not specified in the paper.
missing_details: The paper places this question specifically in Section 11, as part of relating the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks to other theories of wild ramification.

The immediate nearby context is Problem 11.1 and the paragraph stating that the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks can be viewed as another theory of wild ramification in higher dimensions; your draft leaves that framework implicit.

Yasuda’s wording is whether one can “show” such a formula; the paper does not first define a specific Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich-type identity and then ask for its proof. A paper-faithful stand-alone version should therefore allow for both formulation and proof.
The paper says “motivic integration and/or a version of stringy invariant”; your draft’s “or a suitable stringy invariant” is close, but not quite the paper’s formulation.

No specific class of varieties, stacks, covers, sheaves, group actions, or coefficients is fixed in the original problem. A faithful refinement should preserve that intentional generality rather than silently specializing.

Under the standing convention of the paper, the base field is assumed algebraically closed unless specified otherwise, although the author notes that most arguments and problems are valid over any base field.

There are no hidden variables, degree conditions, homogeneity assumptions, nilpotency hypotheses, or “for all sufficiently large m” quantifiers in the original formulation; the missing content is contextual rather than parametric.
refined_question: Within the study of wild ramification considered in the paper—more specifically, in connection with the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks—can one formulate and prove a Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich-type formula using motivic integration and/or a version of stringy invariant?
justification: The draft is clearly targeting Problem 11.2, which matches it almost verbatim. Section 11 first frames the agenda as relating the wild McKay correspondence and motivic integration over wild Deligne-Mumford stacks to other theories of wild ramification, then immediately recalls the Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich formula as a classical result on wild ramification and asks Problem 11.2. Sections 2.2 and 2.3 provide the paper’s operative meanings of “stringy invariant” and “motivic integration” in this context, and the Convention supplies the standing background assumption on the base field. Because the original problem is intentionally broad and does not specify a precise class of objects or a pre-existing formula, the sharpest faithful rewrite is still necessarily somewhat open-ended, but it should explicitly mention the wild McKay/motivic-integration framework from Section 11 rather than only saying “the wild setting.”
